The Boston Red Sox are just a few days away from kicking off a three-game wild-card series against the New York Yankees on the road for the second straight season.
Boston and New York will begin the postseason run on Sep. 29. As the regular season has wrapped up, the biggest red flag for the Red Sox has been their sluggish offense. Throughout the month of September, Boston's offense has been one of the worst in the league. In fact, Boston has scored the fewest runs in baseball in September with just 69 in 23 games. But there is a bright spot, Boston fans. Roman Anthony is starting to look like himself at the plate at the perfect time.
Since Sep. 18, Anthony has batted .357 (10-for-28) with one homer, four doubles and a triple in seven games played. That's the type of production that is going to get the offense back on track. With Willson Contreras up in the air with his hand sore after getting hit by a pitch and Mickey Gasper also getting hurt, Boston needs guys to step up right now. The lights are starting to get bright. Boston has just one more regular season game left on Sunday before the full focus will turn to the playoffs.
Roman Anthony Is Getting Hot
If the Red Sox are going to make a run, they're going to need a lot from Anthony. When healthy, the Red Sox have arguably the deepest lineup in the American League playoffs, but will they actually find a way to get healthy? That's the question. Again, Contreras is up in the air. Gasper hurt his bicep on Friday and the club didn't give an optimistic update in the aftermath. Curtis Mead is on the shelf right now, although he is working his way back. Ceddanne Rafaela missed some time. Masataka Yoshida is on the Injured List as well, and the list goes on and on.
Boston isn't entering the playoffs at full strength, so it needs the guys who are healthy to carry the load to give this club enough time to advance and get closer to full strength. There isn't a guy in the lineup who moves the needle more than Anthony when he's rolling. We've started to see signs of that. If you have Anthony consistently getting on base at the top of the order, there's still enough talent behind him to get some runs in.
Boston's biggest strength is the pitching. The rotation and bullpen have carried the load all season. If they keep pitching as they have, Boston won't need many runs to win games. If Anthony can keep up his recent hot streak, that could be enough to help push Boston forward. He's that impactful.

In a season that will be defined by impactful performances from unlikely sources, Mickey Gasper's rise was the most unbelievable of all.
Yet Gasper's story will not have a postseason, after he suffered a peculiar injury in the Red Sox' third-to-last game of the season.
In the bottom of the fifth inning on Friday afternoon, Gasper swung and missed on a curveball, immediately flexing and grabbing at his right arm on his way to the dugout. He was replaced by Connor Wong, and between games, reports indicated that Gasper's injury was serious.
After the nightcap, manager Chad Tracy confirmed that the injury does appear to be one that will make Gasper unavailable for the postseason.
"At this point, it just looks like a significant biceps injury. So, he's gonna still be seeing more doctors and stuff like that. We'll get a final conclusion, but it's a pretty significant biceps injury," Tracy said. "It's probably gonna take him out."
The 30-year-old Gasper had cooled off since his historic month of August but still figured to be a useful lefty bat for Tracy when the Red Sox take on the Yankees next week for a best-of-three series, beginning on Tuesday. Gasper was catching in Friday's matinee, which would have given Tracy more flexibility in various situations.
Gasper batted .251 with an .823 OPS in 67 games with the Red Sox this season, doing most of his damage in the month of August. That month, he batted .400 with a 1.671 OPS, belting nine extra-base hits in 30 at-bats.
Combined with Willson Contreras declaring himself unlikely to be able to play when the playoffs begin, the Red Sox' lineup has now taken serious hits on consecutive days.
The Yankees are dealing with some injuries, too, though Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton and Trent Grisham are all working toward being able to return for the postseason.

By the time the Red Sox took the field for the second game of Friday’s doubleheader, their postseason destination was already set.
They still found a way to finish a long day at Fenway Park with another win.
Wilyer Abreu snapped an 0-for-11 skid with a two-run double in the eighth inning, while Brayan Bello and Jedixson Paez combined for a shutout as the Red Sox completed a doubleheader sweep of the Cubs with a 2-0 victory.
Boston improved to 87-74 after winning the opener, 4-3, earlier Friday. That victory locked the Red Sox into the No. 5 seed in the American League and officially set up a rematch with the Yankees in the best-of-three Wild Card Series beginning Tuesday at Yankee Stadium.
With the standings no longer a concern, the rest of the weekend is about getting ready for New York.
Abreu entered Game 2 mired in a difficult September, carrying a .622 OPS for the month. He had gone hitless in his first seven at-bats of the doubleheader, including two strikeouts, before stepping to the plate with two outs in the eighth.
This time, Abreu delivered, ripping a two-run double to break a scoreless tie and give Boston a 2-0 lead.
The hit snapped an 0-for-11 skid for Abreu, whose streaky nature has been on display over the past two months. He posted a .971 OPS in August before cooling considerably in September.
After reaching base four times and collecting three extra-base hits in Game 1, Roman Anthony went 1-for-3 with a walk in the nightcap. He finished the doubleheader 4-for-6 with two doubles, a triple and two walks. Over his last six games, Anthony is 10-for-28 (.357) with six extra-base hits.
For an offense that has struggled throughout September, getting its leadoff hitter hot heading into the postseason could provide a significant boost.
The pitching was the bigger story in Game 2, with Bello continuing his impressive turnaround by tossing four scoreless innings against the Cubs.
His season looked much different before a demotion to Triple-A Worcester. Since returning to the majors, Bello has allowed one run or fewer in 12 of his 14 appearances, posting a 2.11 ERA with 13 runs allowed over 55 1/3 innings.
Bello isn’t expected to start during the Wild Card Series, but his work since returning from Worcester has strengthened his case for a spot on the postseason roster, where he could return to his role out of the bullpen.
Paez provided length to the bullpen in Game 2, allowing Chad Tracy to rest his relievers with the travel day coming on Saturday.
The Red Sox recalled the 22-year-old between games after optioning Raymond Burgos, who earned the save with two scoreless innings in the opener.
Paez’s first appearance with Boston on Sept. 1 was one to forget. He surrendered eight runs over 3 2/3 innings against Seattle. Paez replaced Bello and tossed five scoreless innings to finish the game, limiting the Cubs to three hits without issuing a walk while striking out four.
Paez became the first Red Sox pitcher to finish a victory with at least five scoreless innings since Scott Taylor threw 6 2/3 scoreless innings against the Yankees on Oct. 3, 1992. The right-hander is also just the fifth pitcher in franchise history to accomplish the feat within his first five career games and only the second in the last 70 years, joining Taylor.
The Red Sox finished their 2026 slate at Fenway Park with a 41-39 record after sweeping Friday’s doubleheader. Boston also secured its first series victory since Sept. 15, finishing the season 24-26-2 in series play and 11-14-1 at home. The Red Sox won 18 of their final 30 series overall, including 10 of their final 16 at home dating to June 12.
With a nor’easter expected to impact New England this weekend, Major League Baseball moved Sunday’s finale to Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg. The Red Sox and Cubs will fly to Florida following Friday’s doubleheader and play Sunday at 3:05 p.m.
Gasper Likely Out for Wild Card Series
Mickey Gasper will likely miss the Red Sox’ Wild Card Series against the Yankees after suffering a right biceps injury during Friday’s 4-3 win over the Cubs, according to MassLive’s Chris Smith.
The Red Sox officially termed the injury “right biceps discomfort.”
Gasper started behind the plate and appeared to injure his biceps while swinging through a pitch for a strikeout in the fifth inning. He was removed immediately, with Connor Wong replacing him at catcher to begin the sixth.
“I think he’s going over to get an MRI right now,” Tracy said after the game. “He’s in some pretty good discomfort. So I don’t know exactly what it is but he struck out on that last swing and had some discomfort in his biceps.”
Following the Game 2 win, Tracy told reporters that Gasper suffered a significant biceps injury.
Chad Tracy confirms after the game that it looks like a "significant" biceps injury for Mickey Gasper.
"It's probably going to take him out."

Between Boston and Triple-A Worcester, Gasper has hit 19 home runs this season. His likely absence also creates another decision as the Red Sox construct their Wild Card roster.

BOSTON – Injuries have become an all-too-recurring theme for the Red Sox in September, and another one cropped up on Friday when the surging Mickey Gasper injured his right biceps while striking out in the fifth inning of the 4-3 win over the Cubs in Game 1 of a split doubleheader at Fenway Park.
For weeks, there has been a debate if Gasper’s recent power tear would land him a starting spot against righties in the postseason.
There’s a chance it could become a moot point, as Gasper underwent an MRI between games of the twin bill.
When Gasper struck out on a sweeper by Clay Holmes, he immediately started flexing his right arm.
“Some biceps discomfort on that swing,” said Red Sox manager Chad Tracy. “So I think he's going over to get an MRI now and he’s got some pretty good discomfort. So I don't know exactly what it is, but he struck out on that last swing and has discomfort in his bicep.”
Ten of Gasper’s 12 career homers have come in his last 33 games, starting on Aug. 17. He has a 1.082 OPS over that span, covering 106 plate appearances.
It has been a heartwarming rise for the 30-year-old Gasper, a journeyman who spent part of eight seasons in the Minor Leagues.
Gasper, who can also catch, would be an option to replace Contreras if he isn’t ready. But now, Gasper might not be ready either.
“Any time there's an injury and you got stuff going on, it creates uncertainty,” said Tracy. “Obviously we're pushing, and our hope is we get [Contreras] in there, but that creates uncertainty for sure. But as we've done most of the year, whatever actually ends up being the case with all of that, we plan to go play [good] baseball because that's what we’ve been doing all year.”

Looking at Boston Red Sox Catcher Mickey Gasper

With Willson Contreras’ availability for next week’s Wild Card Series already in doubt following a hit-by-pitch to the hand on Sept. 17, the Boston Red Sox could ill afford another hit to their first-base depth.
Which is exactly what happened during Game 1 of Friday’s doubleheader against the visiting Chicago Cubs. Mickey Gasper, serving as catcher and batting second, did not return for the top of the sixth inning, due to right biceps discomfort.
Manager Chad Tracy clarified Gasper felt the discomfort on the swing in his fifth-inning strikeout against Cubs starter Clay Holmes, and said he was going to get an MRI.
“He’s in some pretty good discomfort,” Tracy said.
Gasper has been one of the improbable heroes of this Red Sox season, particularly in the second half. After being recalled from Triple-A Worcester in mid-August, he hit .272 with a 1.119 OPS in 32 games entering Friday. His 22 hits in that span included all 10 of his career home runs.
Contreras has not played since taking a pitch to the top of his hand in Texas on Sept. 17. Though another CT scan on Thursday confirmed there is no fracture, the veteran infielder was unable to swing the bat the last two days due to lingering pain.
But on Friday morning, Tracy said they had not ruled out Contreras playing in the final game of the series.
“Life certainly creates uncertainty,” Tracy said of the Contreras and Gasper injuries. “But like, obviously, we’re pushing. Our hope is we can get them there.”

Alec Gamboa is not a starter. At least not at the Major League level caliber. But when the Red Sox needed someone to open a doubleheader on the last Friday of the regular season, they handed it to him anyway—and the Cubs made him pay for it quickly.
Tyrone Taylor doubled in the first inning to put Chicago on the board. Miguel Amaya followed with a two-run double in the second. Three runs in two innings, Clay Holmes cruising, and the Sox in a hole before most of Fenway (whoever was going to brave the risk of weather) had settled into their seats.
Then the defense took over.
Caleb Durbin threw Matt Shaw out at the plate in the second inning to keep the Cubs from stretching it further. Isiah Kiner-Falefa made a sliding grab in the third. Andruw Monasterio came up with a diving catch in the fourth. Not glamorous plays in the box score, but they kept 3-0 from turning into 5-0, and that mattered later.
Roman Anthony was (finally) doing Roman Anthony things all afternoon. He went 3-for-3 with a walk and his fingerprints are on both comeback sequences that mattered. He got things started in the third when he scored on a Dansby Swanson throwing error to make it 3-1. Stayed alive. Kept the at-bats meaningful.
It stayed there until Adley Rutschman. With two on in the fifth against Caleb Thielbar, Rutschman hit a two-run double to tie the game. That's the at-bat the rest of this recap hangs on. There's no comeback without it.
The Cubs went to Aaron Civale in the seventh. Anthony tripled to right field, then Connor Wong stepped up and hit the go-ahead double. Red Sox 4, Cubs 3.
Willson Contreras didn't play game one—his hand still won't let him swing without pain. Ceddanne Rafaela sat out too. You can file away what Boston did to Chicago's depleted lineup, but you can also file away that a team down 3-0 didn't pack it in. The seventh inning happened.
Game 2 is next. They went ahead and won the first one.
Studs
Roman Anthony — 3-for-3 with a walk. On base four times. Scored on the error in the third to keep Boston in it, tripled in the seventh to set up the go-ahead, and was just relentless all afternoon. This was his game.
Adley Rutschman — utschman's two-run double off Thielbar tied it and gave the whole thing a different shape. That's what you pay for.
Connor Wong — Go-ahead double in the seventh coming in for Mickey Gasper. Simple entry in the ledger, but a needed go-ahead run.
Dud
The first two innings — Three runs on Gamboa before anyone got comfortable. Fair amount of that is on Gamboa, fair amount is just what happens when you open with a reliever and it doesn't work. The Sox survived it. They shouldn't count on that against a full-strength playoff opponent.
The wind — How many times did the wind knock balls down today? Yes for better with potential Cubbies homers knocked down, but also it's a hamper on an already struggling offense for the Sox.
Play of the Game
Rutschman's two-run double in the fifth. Down 3-1, two runners on, Cubs holding a lead that had felt comfortable since the second inning—and Rutschman turned the whole situation. That swing is why the seventh inning got to mean something.

item.content:encoded:
Amid whipping winds and the gathering storm off the coast, the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs embarked upon a doubleheader Friday afternoon.
It looked bleak for the home team early on, as the Cubs took a 3-0 lead during Red Sox rookie left-hander Alec Gamboa’s two-inning opener.
But Roman Anthony is heating up at exactly the right time. His 3 for 3 performance, with two doubles, a triple, walk and two runs carried the Red Sox to a 4-3 win in the top half of the doubleheader.
The victory cemented the Red Sox as the second American League Wild Card team, meaning they are set for a rematch of last year’s Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, which begins Tuesday.
“Just had to find a way to win there, and find a way to just kind of play Red Sox baseball as we’ve done all year, with crazy scheduling and different things,” Anthony said.
Left fielder Tyrone Taylor gave the Cubs an instant lead in the first, with a two-out RBI double after Gamboa’s one-out walk to right-fielder Seiya Suzuki. First baseman Michael Busch and shortstop Dansby Swanson slid headfirst into home in rapid succession when catcher Miguel Amaya doubled with one out in the second for a 3-0 lead.
Southpaw Jake Bennett, a starter for all 19 games of this rookie season, replaced Gamboa in the third. Bennett’s first major league relief effort encompassed 3 2/3 scoreless innings in which he yielded three hits, walked one and struck out one.
“He looked very comfortable, and was able to get in the zone right away,” Red Sox manager Chad Tracy said.
“Definitely a little bit of an adrenaline rush, but at the end of the day it’s the same game,” Bennett said of the difference between starting and relieving. “Just in the case that I have to come out of the bullpen in the wild card, just good to have some experience doing it at this level.”
Righty Greg Weissert (1 1/3 IP) and lefty Raymond Burgos (2 IP) held the Cubs off the rest of the way.
The Red Sox pitching staff entered Friday with 41 games with one or zero runs allowed, not only the most in the majors this season, but the club’s most in a season since the Live-Ball Era began in 1920. The Red Sox entered Friday with the third-best ERA in MLB. If they can hang on through the rest of the weekend, it will be their first season in the top three since 2007.
The bats have been Boston’s bigger issue this month, and most of the season, by far. Through 22 September games including Game 1 on Friday, the Red Sox are averaging 7.5 runners left on base per game, matching their dismal May mark.
Yet, the Red Sox were 2 for 13 with runners in scoring position, and left eight men on base, but they outhit the Cubs, 9-7, drew four walks and only struck out four times for an improvement over recent games.
“Quite a few guys that swung the bats well, we got tons of big hits, especially in the second part of the game,” Tracy said. “It was a really good offensive showing, for sure.”
After his wasted leadoff double in the first, Anthony scored the only Red Sox run through four innings, on Swanson’s throwing error in the bottom of the third.
Anthony’s second double off Cubs starter Clay Holmes went to better use. He followed Isiah Kiner-Falefa’s leadoff single in the fifth, and both men scored when designated hitter Adley Rutschman greeted lefty reliever Caleb Thielbar with a two-run single.
Holmes, a longtime New York Yankee, went 4 1/3 innings on 78 pitches (50 strikes). He allowed three runs, two earned, on five hits, walked three and struck out three.
Red Sox catcher Mickey Gasper was Holmes’ final batter. After striking out against Holmes for the third time, Gasper was replaced at catcher by Connor Wong for the top of the sixth due to what the Red Sox later announced as right biceps discomfort.
“He’s in some pretty good discomfort,” Tracy said of Gasper, who underwent an MRI after the game.
Wong’s entry proved otherwise fortuitous in the bottom of the seventh. His 12th double of the year rocketed down the third-base line, and Anthony, who tripled, jogged home for the go-ahead run.
That Anthony used the whole field with a double to left, double to center, and triple to right was among the most encouraging aspects of his offensive showing. Particularly as the swirling winds sent balls flying in unusual directions throughout the game.
“When I’m using that other way, that’s the biggest thing for me, I’ve had a lot of success in the past, and when I’m going well, I’m hitting it where it’s pitched, and taking advantage of that wall over there, even on windy days like today,” Anthony said. “Just kind of continue to pass it along, and try to be just a problem (for pitchers) any way that you possibly can.”
It fell to Burgos to protect the one-run lead in the ninth. The Red Sox southpaw did so with a 1-2-3 inning that included winning a 10-pitch at-bat against National League MVP favorite Pete Crow-Armstrong for the second out.
The Red Sox are 86-74, with two regular-season games left to play.
After that, they’re on to New York.

Mickey Gasper stepped up to the plate in the fifth inning on a windy day in Boston and worked the count full. He gave an aggressive swing on the sixth pitch he saw for a strikeout with two runners on base, but that isn't the worst of it.
Gasper winced after his big swing. On his walk back to the Boston Red Sox's dugout, he flexed his arm and bent his elbow. He pressed his bicep, looking for an issue. A trainer examined him in the dugout before he went down the tunnel and left the game. Connor Wong replaced Gasper behind the dish.
Gasper left the game with biceps discomfort, according to multiple sources including Tim Healey of The Boston Globe. That's a vague diagnosis, but any further injuries are an ugly sign for the Sox. Willson Contreras has been sidelined since he was hit in the hand by a pitch on September 17, just four games after he returned from the injured list with a hamstring injury. The first baseman isn't confident he'll be available for the Wild Card round, and Boston needs all the offensive help it can get without him.
Gasper has cooled down lately, but he's recently off an incredible stint at the plate in the second half of August. He slashed .400/.571/1.100 with three doubles, six home runs and 10 RBI over 12 games last month.
Mickey Gasper pulled from first game of Cubs-Red Sox doubleheader with apparent arm injury following big swing
Even if Gasper has slowed down offensively, he's still proven a home run threat since his red-hot month. He's hit four homers in September, one as recently as September 22, while slashing .196/.328/.451.
If Gasper can't return to play this season, Boston has a few replacement options with the "stay ready" squad in Fort Myers. Romy Gonzalez was scorching with the WooSox in September to the tune of a .371/.410/.571 slash line. Braiden Ward and Tsung-Che Cheng are also there, but Gonzalez is the best pick given his MLB experience and recent heater. He also crushes lefties and the New York Yankees are sure to throw at least two the Red Sox's way during the Wild Card round.
Top prospect Franklin Arias is also part of the Fort Myers squad and he was in Boston on the night of September 24. item.content:encoded:
There was the 1-0 loss to the Guardians. There were the weather updates that might very well have the Red Sox and Cubs playing somewhere other than Fenway Park this weekend. And there was Ceddanne Rafaela's return from his hamstring scare.
But when it came to news that mattered for the Red Sox, it was hard to top what Willson Contreras said after this latest defeat.
The first baseman's bruised right hand evidently does not seem to be cooperating when it comes to postseason readiness.
"I mean, it's really concerning,” Contreras said. “But at the same time, I'm putting all my effort -- and everything I can do, I'm doing it. I don't know what else to say. I’m working hard with the trainers; the hand is slowly getting better. But I haven’t been able to swing the last two days. I’ll be honest with the team. I know Tuesday is a really important game. It's a really important series, and I'll be completely honest with the team.”
Contreras added, "It's frustrating, if I’m being honest. I was hoping to swing today, and I couldn't swing. I came into my locker just tearing up because that's what we play for. We play to play in October, and it's really frustrating when we're doing the best you can do and you're expecting to heal faster and that doesn't happen."
It appeared as though Contreras was headed in the right direction, taking an exorbitant amount of swings prior to Tuesday's game, both on the Fenway field and underneath with the Trajekt pitching machine. But the results from the exercise were not positive, with the righty hitter unable to replicate any sort of batting practice over the last couple of days.
There is still time for Contreras, with the Red Sox's first wild-card game on Tuesday. But his original plan to use the weekend games against the Cubs as a tune-up for the playoffs seems extremely unlikely.
Why is this such a big deal? It's because of the skill-set Contreras carries, one that the Red Sox seem starved for heading into the postseason.
All good postseason runs are usually built on the back of top-of-the-order power, with opponents needing to navigate their way through a team's alpha batters. Hitting home runs, in particular, is usually a top priority. The Blue Jays and Dodgers lived that life a year ago, as did the Yankees and Los Angeles the year before. You know who didn't? The 2025 Red Sox during their three wild-card games at Yankee Stadium.
Trevor Story's solo homer in Game 2 of last season's playoff showdown with the Yankees marked the only time a Red Sox player cleared the fences. It was a deficiency that was difficult to ignore.
It was why Craig Breslow proclaimed early in the offseason that his team needed more power. It was the reason acquiring Curtis Mead became a priority heading into the trade deadline. And it is why Contreras, who leads the Red Sox with 27 homers, has been so important. (The Red Sox are 18-8 when Contreras hits at least one homer.)
While this Red Sox team has taught us that things can turn in a hurry, the way the Sox's offense has been trending isn't good. In the last five games, the Sox have hit only two home runs. And in September, Chad Tracy's team has the second-lowest batting average and OPS in baseball, while scoring the fewest runs (13 fewer than the next-worst).
There are potential solutions to the Red Sox's postseason power problem, including Roman Anthony (who is tied with Mickey Gasper for the team lead in homers for September with four), Adley Rutschman, Story, Rafaela and Wilyer Abreu, who has two home runs since Aug. 16.
But Contreras has always been the constant ... until now.
“When it hurts, it hurts. Especially when it's the top hand,” Contreras said. “If it was the bottom hand, I could swing with the right hand, but when it's the right hand, my right hand just feels weaker until I just let the bat go. It's not a good sign. ... Again, I'm doing everything that I can to come back and play with the boys and be there with the boys. But sometimes you have to listen to your body, and I'm listening to the trainers and doing everything that they ask me to do, and [it's] just one of those things that I can't control."

The Boston Red Sox’s game on Thursday didn’t mean much. But after a 1-0 loss to the Cleveland Guardians, the fan base got a much worse gut punch.
All-Star first baseman Willson Contreras, who has been Boston’s best hitter all season, has been working to return from a hand injury sustained on a wild pitch last Thursday. He was seen taking batting practice on the field earlier this week at Fenway Park, but evidently, he’s not feeling close to 100%.
Contreras told the media on Thursday night that he was unable to swing on Wednesday or Thursday due to the slow recovery he had after Tuesday’s batting practice session. With only five days until the playoffs begin, that leaves the Red Sox working against the clock.
Contreras doesn’t sound optimistic about playoffs
Worst of all, Contreras’ language postgame made it seem as if he was already anticipating that he wouldn’t be able to take the field on Tuesday, likely in the Bronx against the arch-rival New York Yankees.
"I mean it's frustrating, being honest. I was hoping to swing today. Couldn't swing, I came into my locker, I was tearing up. I'm being honest," Contreras said, via Michael Hurley of NBC Sports Boston. "Because that's what we play for. We play to play in October … and it's really frustrating when you're doing the best you can do and you're expecting to heal faster and that doesn't happen."
Anything can happen in a three-game series, but the Red Sox would be at a serious disadvantage without Contreras, their team leader in most offensive categories. It makes the situation all the more painful that Contreras had just worked his way back from a stint on the injured list for a hamstring issue, which he’d played through for most of the season.
If Contreras isn’t able to go, the Red Sox have their pick between Nick Sogard and Mickey Gasper at first base on the current roster, and there might be a spot for Romy Gonzalez to return from Triple-A to fill a void against left-handed pitching at the position. All of those guys are capable of helping out, but none have the consistency or power potential of Contreras.
It’s a developing story, but Thursday was a tough pill to swallow for the Red Sox and their fans. All Contreras can do is keep working, and as long as he’s out, the Red Sox have to do all in their power to stave off elimination and earn him more games to play.

The Boston Red Sox kept outfielder Jarren Duran out of the starting lineup again Wednesday night as they hosted the Cleveland Guardians in the second game of a three-game series at Fenway Park.
Manager Chad Tracy’s posted batting order featured Roman Anthony in left field, Nick Sogard at first base, Jahmai Jones as the designated hitter, Wilyer Abreu in right field, Adley Rutschman behind the plate, Ceddanne Rafaela in center field, Caleb Durbin at third base, Trevor Story at shortstop and Andruw Monasterio at second base. Sonny Gray was listed as the starting pitcher.
Duran also sat Tuesday, when the Guardians beat the Red Sox 3-2. He entered that game as a pinch-hitter and drew a walk.
Cleveland took the series opener on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly in the ninth inning. The Guardians stranded 15 runners but still extended their winning streak to six games.
Boston dropped to 84-73. The club already clinched an American League Wild Card berth Sunday but has lost three straight and eight of its last 12.
Duran entered Wednesday batting .204 with 110 hits, 20 home runs, 69 RBIs, 65 runs and 19 stolen bases in 146 games. He had 538 at-bats, 39 walks and 163 strikeouts.
The left-handed hitter has struggled in September. He was 9-for-50 with one home run and one RBI in 17 games this month before Tuesday’s appearance.
Over his last 15 games he was 8-for-42 with one homer. His on-base-plus-slugging percentage sat at .625 for the season.
Rafaela’s return to center field tightened the outfield picture. Anthony has been starting in left and Abreu in right, leaving Duran as the extra outfielder in many recent games.
Tracy had the interim tag removed Tuesday and was named the franchise’s 49th manager. The Red Sox have used a mix of platoons and rest days for Duran down the stretch.
Gray brings a 17-5 record and 2.82 ERA into the start. Cleveland is expected to counter with Forrest Griffin.
The Guardians sit at 82-75 and hold a one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox in the AL Central. Chicago owns the season-series tiebreaker.
Duran, 30, is in his sixth major league season, all with Boston. He was an All-Star in 2024.
He still ranks among the team leaders in home runs and RBIs despite the low batting average. His 20 homers leave him one short of his career high.
The Red Sox close the regular season with this series, then host the Chicago Cubs for three games. Seeding and rest for the Wild Card round remain in play.
Duran’s speed and defense have kept him in the mix even as his batting average dropped. He stole 19 bases and continued to play a plus outfield when used.
Boston’s offense produced eight hits Tuesday. Rutschman went 3-for-4 and pinch-hitter Mickey Gasper tied the game with a home run in the eighth.
Cleveland collected 12 hits. Angel Martínez finished 3-for-4.
The Red Sox sit 12 games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the AL East. The Yankees hold the other Wild Card spot six games ahead of Boston.
Duran’s role for the final week and any postseason series will depend on how Tracy balances the four outfielders available.

The Yankees had to make do without Aaron Judge for all of June, July and August due to a stress fracture in his right first rib. With the days on the calendar dwindling and the AL East title still in play — which is no longer the case after the Rays clinched on Tuesday night — Judge bypassed a rehab assignment, but once he returned, he played in just seven games before landing back on the injured list due to a right calf strain. Both the slugger and the team took great pains to avoid discussing the injury’s specificity and timeline for recovery until Tuesday, when manager Aaron Boone revealed that Judge has a “moderate grade” strain, received a platelet-poor plasma injection, and isn’t expected to be available for the team’s Wild Card Series rematch against the Red Sox.
While deadline acquisition Heliot Ramos has heated up after a very slow start to his pinstriped career, the Yankees’ right field situation is one of the more glaring potential trouble spots among American League contenders. As the playoffs approach, teams no longer have a chance to upgrade from outside their organizations and instead must make do with the talent on hand. What follows here is a look at the most vulnerable teams at each position — something of a companion to my annual pre-deadline Replacement Level Killers series, with a focus on the teams that still have a chance to make the playoffs. For the AL, that means the Rays, Yankees, and Red Sox — all of whom have clinched spots — plus the Guardians, White Sox, Rangers, and Astros, who are battling for the other two division titles and the third Wild Card spot. I’ve taken the Blue Jays out of consideration, as their Playoff Odds now start with a zero in front of the decimal. While full-season performances play a significant part here, I’m more concerned with who’s worst now, with injuries and adjustments in mind. Each position has a headliner (or two, if it’s a job share), but at several positions, I’ve noted other teams with concerns. A companion National League piece will follow.
Catcher: Kyle Teel and Jake Rogers, White Sox
A Top 100 prospect in both 2024 and ’25, Kyle Teel did a very solid job as a rookie last season, hitting for a 125 wRC+ with 1.9 WAR in just 78 games, but he missed the first two months of this season due to a Grade 2 right hamstring strain and then an LCL sprain in his right knee. His replacements, mainly Edgar Quero (a three-time Top 100 prospect) and Drew Romo, struggled so mightily that they headed the catchers’ section on my Replacement Level Killers list, with Quero optioned to Triple-A Charlotte once Teel returned. While Teel’s defense has been an upgrade, he’s hit just .178/.302/.318 (81 wRC+) with an astronomical 37.3% strikeout rate, up from last year’s 25.9%, and his average exit velocity is just 84.5 mph, down from last year’s 88.3 mph. He recently missed time with a left ankle sprain as well.
Romo was optioned to Charlotte in early September during a shuffle that included both Teel’s return and the arrival of the 31-year-old Jake Rogers via the waiver wire. Rogers, who began the year with the Tigers, was traded to the Orioles in late July, then flipped to the Red Sox in the Adley Rutschman trade on August 3 before being sent on his merry way again within a fortnight. He’s now playing for his fourth team this season and has hit just .161/.276/.287 (62 wRC+). All told, White Sox catchers have combined for a 54 wRC+ and -0.4 WAR, both of which rank 29th in the majors; for as much long-term potential as the 24-year-old Teel and 23-year-old Quero (who has played sparingly since being recalled) may have, they’re less than ideal right now.
It’s worth noting that Rutschman, who was on the injured list due to left wrist inflammation when he was sent to Boston as part of a seven-player blockbuster, has struggled to the point that he’s a concern as well. The 28-year-old switch-hitter was batting a solid .251/.331/.433 (116 wRC+) before being sidelined for three weeks — his third IL stint this season, with shorter ones for left ankle inflammation and a concussion while with Baltimore — but he’s hit just .214/.270/.398 (82 wRC+) in 111 plate appearances since being activated. His strikeout rate has spiked from 14.1% to 21.6%, and his average exit velo has fallen by about two ticks. Backup Connor Wong has hit a similarly light .234/.310/.346 (84 wRC+), albeit with dreadful defense (-10 FRV, -8 DRS, -6.6 FRM). The good news is that Rutschman went 3-for-4 with a pair of doubles on Tuesday night against the Guardians; the bad news is that the Red Sox have other injury concerns in their lineup as well.
First Base: Nathaniel Lowe and David Fry, Guardians
Guardians first basemen made my Killers list due to the light production of their platoon of Kyle Manzardo and Rhys Hoskins. At the deadline, they dealt for Nathaniel Lowe and optioned Manzardo to Triple-A Columbus. A couple of week later, they placed Hoskins on the IL due to lower back inflammation and turned to David Fry, a utilityman who can catch. Alas, after getting a 94 wRC+ from their first basemen prior to the deadline, they’ve managed just a 90 wRC+ since. The lefty-swinging Lowe, who hit a robust .266/.341/.480 (123 wRC+) for the Reds, has dipped to .228/.279/.390 (83 wRC+) while hitting a ton of popups. The righty-swinging Fry has done well in his limited duty at first base, but has hit just .192/.312/.349 (90 wRC+) in 202 plate appearances overall.
Hoskins began a swing progression nearly two weeks ago, but with Columbus’ season having ended, a rehab assignment isn’t an option, which doesn’t bode well for an uptick from his .179/.306/.376 (95 wRC+) line. Manzardo (.215/.306/.378, 95 wRC+) didn’t hit the ball as hard at Columbus as he had either in his previous stops there or in Cleveland, and there hasn’t been any buzz about bringing him back in September or October.
Meanwhile in Boston, Willson Contreras has been the team’s top hitter, batting a potent .276/.387/.518 (152 wRC+) with 27 homers, but he’s been limited to four games this month between a left hamstring strain and a hit-by-pitch induced bruised knuckle on his right hand. Fortunately, he avoided a fracture, and returned to swinging a bat on September 20; the Red Sox hope to get him into the lineup before the end of the regular season, but the situation bears monitoring. Mickey Gasper and Nick Sogard have shared duties during his absence. Both have provided above-average production overall; Gasper had been in a 4-for-32 slump before hitting a pinch-homer — his 10th long ball in 218 plate appearances — against the Guardians on Tuesday night.
Second Base: Jose Altuve, Astros
Jose Altuve may wind up in Cooperstown some day, but Father Time has caught up to the diminutive 36-year-old. He’s batting just .250/.308/.402, which has taken a bite out of both the Astros’ offense and his chances at reaching 3,000 hits; his 99 wRC+ is his lowest full-season mark since 2013, while his .327 xSLG is a 57-point drop from last season and a Statcast-era low. What’s more, his defense has reached its nadir, with both his -10 FRV and -16 DRS rating not only as career worsts but also major league worsts at his position. With Yordan Alvarez entrenched at designated hitter and too valuable to risk in left field — he hasn’t used his glove in a postseason game since 2023 — there’s no place to hide Altuve, but also little likelihood he’ll be benched in favor of backup Nick Allen (.271/.318/.371, 95 wRC+).
On the injury front, keep an eye on the return of the Yankees’ Jazz Chisholm Jr., who was activated between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Rays after missing 12 games due to a sprained right thumb. While his offense has dipped from a 125 wRC+ last year to 100 (.233/.313/.403) this year, Chisholm’s 3.4 WAR ranks third among the team’s position players behind Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, and his total of 19 home runs ranks second. Backups Anthony Volpe (.244/.321/.335, 88 wRC+) and José Caballero (.236/.293/.373, 86 wRC+) are substantial steps down, but if Chisholm has any lingering issues, one of them may be needed to fill in.
Third Base: Ryan McMahon and Amed Rosario, Yankees
Yankees third basemen have combined for -0.1 WAR, the majors’ third-lowest mark. Lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon bears the bulk of the responsibility for that, hitting just .206/.274/.341 (73 wRC+) while playing solid defense. Righty-swinging Amed Rosario has produced a 100 wRC+ while playing third but has hit just .233/.275/.406 (87 wRC+) overall, and he’s been lousy at the hot corner, with -6 DRS and -6 FRV in just 309.1 innings. The righty-swinging Caballero is at least a better defender than Rosario and about on par offensively, and he’s one of the league’s top base thieves, with 34 steals in 45 attempts. He has also out-produced Rosario against lefties, with an 81 wRC+ to Rosario’s 63 — which could be a factor given that the Red Sox can call upon lefties Ranger Suarez and Payton Tolle to start during the Wild Card Series.
Shortstop: Taylor Walls, Rays
For the third year in a row, the defensive metrics have been very split with regards to Taylor Walls. His 21 DRS leads all shortstops (nobody else has more than 10 DRS), but his -2 FRV ranks 23rd out of 30 with at least 500 innings at the position. Between the latter mark and his dismal .222/.308/.294 (73 wRC+) line, he’s produced just 0.7 WAR. That said, neither Jorge Mateo (.205/.250/.318, 55 wRC+) nor Ben Williamson (.244/.304/.327, 79 wRC+), his occasional fill-ins, hits well enough to merit surpassing Wells on the depth chart.
Left Field: Taylor Trammell and LaMonte Wade Jr., Astros
The Astros’ current 1.3 WAR from their left fielders ranks 17th in the majors, ahead of both the Guardians (1.2) and Red Sox (0.8). But between Steven Kwan’s second-half heater and Roman Anthony’s return from a torn tendon in his right ring finger, both of those teams are now in a better spot than Houston. Taylor Trammell made several Top 100 lists as a prospect — he was as high as no. 12 as a 60-FV on our 2019 list — but he’s now 29 and has netted 0.1 WAR in 273 major league games for four different teams. This year he’s hit .200/.292/.355 (84 wRC+) in a career-high 95 games spread across the three outfield positions, with a 95 wRC+ in 237 plate appearances against righties and a 19 wRC+ (ouch) in 41 plate appearances against lefties.
LaMonte Wade Jr., a reliable contributor for the Giants from 2021–24, bottomed out to a 53 wRC+ last year in a season split between San Francisco and Anaheim. He spent the first few months of this season in the White Sox organization but was released on June 1 so he could sign with the Astros, for whom he’s hit .208/.308/.352 (90 wRC+). He’s been protected from facing many lefties and has seen his playing time dry up otherwise, as he’s been in a slump since mid-August. Meanwhile, righty-swinging Nelson Velázquez hasn’t made a very strong case for himself by hitting .192/.255/.414 (81 wRC+) with a 33.6% strikeout rate in 110 plate appearances split between the Cardinals and Astros. With options like these, you can see why playing Alvarez in left and DHing Altuve starts to make some sense.
Center Field: Daulton Varsho, Astros
The first-half struggles of Jake Meyers, Brice Matthews and Trammell landed the Astros on the Killers center field list, so they quite reasonably dealt for Daulton Varsho on August 3. The 30-year-old flychaser was hitting .243/.307/.375 (91 wRC+), and while his once-elite defense has regressed towards average, a performance like that is still good enough to carry the position. He looked like a decent upgrade for Houston, but while his defense has remained solid enough, he’s hit an anemic .172/.224/.311 (48 wRC+), with his strikeout and walk rates both moving in the wrong direction.
A closer look shows that Varsho has actually been hitting the ball slightly harder since the trade, but all season, he’s been producing popups and cans of corn galore because he’s getting under so many pitches. The real fall-off is relative to last year; his pulled air rate has fallen from 29.5% to 18.5%, while his xSLG has dropped from .464 to .354. As with Altuve and the left field situation, the Astros don’t have great alternatives. Matthews, a 24-year-old rookie, has hit just .201/.255/.332 (64 wRC+), and Meyers sustained a season-ending left kneecap injury at Triple-A Sugar Land last week.
Yet another injury-related note for the Red Sox: Ceddanne Rafaela was sidelined nearly three weeks ago due to a right quad strain. Prior to that, he was putting the finishing touches on a breakout season, having hit .282/.317/.443 (108 wRC+) with 16 homers and 17 steals while playing Gold Glove-caliber defense in center field. Less than a week after he went down, his capable fill-in Eli White suffered a ligament injury in his right foot, requiring season-ending surgery. Since then, Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton have shared the position. Rafaela has yet to return to the roster, though manager Chad Tracy said he’s “getting close.” If he does suffer a setback, continuing to play Duran during what’s been an awful season (.204/.261/.362, 68 wRC+) would obviously be less than ideal.
The Yankees’ Trent Grisham was sidelined by a Grade 2 strain of his right hamstring around the same time that Rafaela went down, and he has yet to return as well. His performance has fallen off drastically after a career year; he’s hit just .211/.308/.395 (98 wRC+) with 18 homers while trading some power for contact, and his defense has also been rough (-5 FRV and -8 DRS in 961.1 innings). While Boone has said he could be “in play at some point” during the postseason, there’s little urgency. Rookie Spencer Jones has shifted over from right field and done an impressive job of holding down the fort, playing adequate defense while hitting .246/.316/.435 (110 wRC+) despite a 36.2% strikeout rate.
Right Field: Heliot Ramos and Aaron Judge, Yankees
Yes, that looks weird in print, but for the moment at least, it’s a reality for the Yankees. The 27-year-old Ramos hit a modest .264/.304/.424 (100 wRC+) with nine homers and 0.6 WAR for the Giants before being traded to the Yankees on August 3. He began his time in pinstripes by going 5-for-47, and at one point went 32 games between homers — from July 20 to August 29 — while slugging .204. He’s heated up since then, but his .168/.294/.356 (85 wRC+) line with the Yankees doesn’t give anyone much confidence he can replace even the banged-up version of Judge the Yankees have received in his 66 games this season (.241/.360/.511, 141 wRC+).
In terms of concerns about sheer replacement-level production, the White Sox stand out here. Early in the season, the team tried Everson Pereira, Jarred Kelenic, and Rikuu Nishida as their regular at the position, but none got the job done. On June 9 they called up Braden Montgomery, a switch-hitting 23-year-old who placed 100th on our Top 100 as a 50-FV prospect in the spring. He collected two hits in his debut that night against the Braves, capped by a walk-off homer, but it’s been mostly downhill since then, as he’s hit .212/.305/.340 (84 wRC+) with six homers and 0.5 WAR in 88 games. While he’s hit .248/.344/.385 (110 wRC+) in 250 plate appearances against righties, he’s flailed away at a .125/.204/.2227 clip in 98 plate appearances against lefties. With resurgent lefty-masher Randal Grichuk on the roster and hitting .331/.372/.650 (182 wRC+) in 172 plate appearances against lefties, there’s no reason that should be happening.
Designated Hitter: Andrew Benintendi, White Sox
No remaining AL contender ranks below 15th in the majors in wRC+ provided by their DHs, and the two lowest teams from among that subset, the Red Sox and Guardians, are respectively third and fourth in second-half wRC+ from that spot while using revolving casts of players. So I’m picking (on) Andrew Benintendi, who has hit a very modest .243/.302/.414 (98 wRC+) while starting at DH in 105 games, with Grichuk (19) the only other Chicago player in double digits. There’s nothing particularly terrible or mysterious about Benintendi’s performance, which beyond a September slump, has lined up with his expected stats quite well; he’s got 21st-percentile bat speed but a 66th-percentile squared-up rate and a 77th-percentile hard-hit rate. He doesn’t hit lefties (.227/.261/.250, 44 wRC+ in 47 PA this year), so manager Will Venable has either used Grichuk or one of his righty regulars there. For as impressive as the White Sox’s turnaround from three straight 100-loss seasons has been, you can see from this roundup that the team’s weaknesses have come to the fore as they’ve tried to sew up a playoff berth.

The Boston Red Sox clinched their second consecutive playoff berth Sunday and their third since 2021.
It was a season with the highest of highs and the lowest of lows in Boston as they started the season 10-17 before firing longtime manager Alex Cora.
In June, the Red Sox found themselves 14 games under .500 at a record of 32-46. This is when everything changed.
They swept the New York Yankees before losing two out of three games to the Washington Nationals.
The Red Sox went on the road and swept the Los Angeles Angels, Chicago White Sox and New York Mets to sit at 46-48 heading into the all-star break.
After nine straight road wins, the Red Sox headed home to face the 56-38 Tampa Bay Rays. Tampa has had Boston’s number in the past few seasons, but this weekend was different.
In the first game of a doubleheader after the break, the Red Sox took care of business 10-0. Then in the night cap, Tampa Bay Rays took an early 2-0 before outfielder Wilyer Abreu decided the next 24 hours were all about him. He hit two home runs on the way to a 5-3 Red Sox win.
The next game was the defining game of the winning streak. The Rays were matching the Sox in scoring all-game before Abreu stepped to the plate down 6-5 in the seventh. Abreu crushed a two-run homer to right field, sending himself and Fenway Park into a frenzy. His fourth home run in 24 hours put Boston up 7-6, a lead they would hold for 12 consecutive wins.
They swept Tampa the next day before taking the first two games of the series versus the Orioles to tie a franchise record 15 straight wins. That first win did not come without drama. A back-and-forth game was knotted up in the eighth when Caleb Durbin smacked a game winning homerun to left field. The “Durbinator” had a rough start to the season but became one of the centerpieces of this win streak.
The streak would end at 15 but just a week later, Boston would rip off another nine straight wins. Durbin hit a walk-off single in an instant classic 12-11 victory against the White Sox. Ceddanne Rafaela became the king of LA for a few days after smacking four home runs in three games against the back-to-back champs.
So here we are, the Red Sox are 84-72 with a firm grip on the second wild card spot in the American League. Now, the New York Yankees stand in their way.
The Yankees beat the Red Sox 2-1 in the three-game wildcard series last year, and Boston is looking for revenge this season.
The pitching will be the key for both teams. Payton Tolle, Sonny Gray and Ranger Suarez will toe the rubber for Boston against the Yankees’ Gerritt Cole, Max Fried and Massachusetts’ own Cam Schlittler in the series.
In his first full season in the MLB, Tolle hit his stride. The southpaw posted a 3.02 ERA and a 10.4 K/9. He is also peaking at the right time, sporting a 0.75 ERA in two starts during September.
In a complete 180 from Tolle, Gray has been dominant in what may be his swan song in the majors. After being acquired via trade in the offseason, Gray has won 17 games, a career high for the veteran. He pitched 7.1 innings of one hit baseball while striking out nine in a June win over the Yankees.
Suarez signed a 5-year $130 million dollar contract with Boston in the offseason and has been solid as a member of the Sox. However, the 2026 all-star struggled in all three of his starts against the Yankees. The Bronx Bombers were 3-0 against Suarez.
Despite great performances by the Yankees, Suarez is a playoff pitcher. He had a 1.48 ERA in 42.2 postseason innings as a member of the Philadelphia Phillies. In Philadelphia’s 2022 run to the World Series, the Phillies won all five games Suarez pitched in. He only allowed two earned runs in 14.2 innings pitched in 2022.
Along with the starters, the back of the bullpen has been nails for Boston. Erik Miller, Garrett Whitlock and Aroldis Chapman handled the seventh, eighth and ninth innings for interim manager Chad Tracy and the Red Sox. Miller came over at the trade deadline and did not allow an earned run in his first 10 appearances. Whitlock has been a staple in the Red Sox bullpen since 2021 and is possibly having his best year yet. He has a 1.75 ERA in 53 appearances. Chapman continues to age like fine wine. The 38-year-old was named an all-star for the second straight year and is 34/36 in save situations this year.
The rest of the hitters for the Red Sox will need to do some heavy lifting if they want to compete with the Yankees. Boston acquired Adley Rutschman at the deadline, and the catcher will be required to switch hit and catch in the playoffs. Wilson Contreras and Trevor Story will add postseason experience to the lineup while former top prospect Roman Anthony and local legend Mickey Gasper will look to provide during their first playoff at bats.
If the standings hold, the Red Sox and Yankees will battle in the Bronx on Tuesday for the wildcard series, a statement no Red Sox fan would have believed in June.

The Boston Red Sox haven't been playing their best overall baseball over the last few weeks in the lead-up to the postseason. Arguably, the biggest reason for this is the fact that they have been navigating a few difficult injuries.
For example, center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela hasn't played in a game since Sep. 2 due to a right quadriceps strain. That is expected to change on Wednesday. After the Red Sox's loss against the Cleveland Guardians on Tuesday, Boston manager Chad Tracy shared that Rafaela is expected to be activated off the Injured List on Wednesday and that Willson Contreras has been taking batting practice, as shared on X by The Athletic's Jen McCaffrey.
The Red Sox Are Going To Get A Boost
"Chad Tracy expects Ceddanne Rafaela to be back in the lineup tomorrow. Willson Contreras took BP but still day to day," McCaffrey wrote on X.
Before Rafaela landed on the Injured List, he was smack dab in the middle of the best season of his career to this point. On top of playing Gold Glove Award-level defense in center field, Rafaela was slashing .282/.317/.443 with a .760 OPS, 16 homers, 70 RBIs, 17 stolen bases, 32 doubles and three triples in 135 games played. Rafaela's return shouldn't be understated. This is big news for the Red Sox.
Rafaela has racked up 5.4 wins above replacement this season, which is a new career high. Rafaela has the second-highest total on the Red Sox's roster and is tied for 22nd in baseball in general. If he didn't miss almost a month of action, he'd be much higher as well.
With Rafaela back in the mix, they can slot him in comfortably in center field and near the top of the lineup. With him in center field over guys like Jarren Duran and Nate Eaton. Duran has gotten a chunk of time there since Rafaela got hurt. With center field now full, then it's going to be a question each night whether Boston wants to roll with Duran in left field and Roman Anthony as the DH, or Anthony in left field and then make a decision at DH.
The outfield logjam situation was something that hung over the Red Sox to begin the season. Now, it's a bit different. If the Red Sox were to stick Anthony in left field, there's a good chance that it wouldn't be Duran as the DH. He has shown very solid pop this season, but with five games left, he's batting .204.
Instead, the Red Sox could slide someone, like Mickey Gasper, into the spot. Gasper specifically is batting .259 and bashed his 10th homer of the season on Tuesday. With Rafaela back, Boston's lineup overall can be better. The offense has taken a hit recently, Rafaela is the guy who is going to boost it. Rafaela is going to help himself, and his return could get a struggling bat out of the lineup on a nightly basis. Two positives.

BOSTON — Nathaniel Lowe had a tiebreaking sacrifice fly off reliever Erik Miller in the ninth inning, and the Cleveland Guardians maintained their slim in the AL Central with a 3-2 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Tuesday night.
Angel Martínez had three hits for the Guardians, who entered the day with a one-game lead over the White Sox atop the division. Chicago owns the tiebreaker by winning the season series. Cleveland stranded 15 baserunners.
The loss was Boston’s eighth in 12 games, spoiling Chad Tracy’s first game as manager after the club named him its 49th in team history.
Adley Rutschman added three hits for Boston, which clinched one of the AL’s wild-card spots on Sunday.
Boston pinch hitter Mickey Gasper hit Hunter Gaddis’ first pitch, tying it at 2-2 leading off the eighth.
Gaddis (5-3) got the win and Cade Smith recorded the final three outs for his 40th save.
Miller (4-2) hit a batter and gave up two hits in an inning.
A strong candidate for the AL Rookie of the Year, Cleveland left-hander Parker Messick gave up a run over five innings. He lowered his ERA to 2.55 and is on pace to become the fourth rookie starting pitcher in MLB history with an ERA under 2.60 and averaging 9.0 or more strikeouts per nine innings.
In his tune-up for a likely playoff start next week, Boston lefty Payton Tolle struggled with his control over 5 2/3 innings, giving up two runs on eight hits.
Up next
Guardians LHP Foster Griffin (15-5, 3.67 ERA) is set to face Red Sox RHP Sonny Gray (17-5, 2.82) on Wednesday in the middle game of the three-game series.

item.content:encoded:
In this purgatorial period for the Red Sox, after they clinched a playoff berth over the weekend and before they open the postseason next week, what matters?
The result Tuesday, a 3-2 loss to the Guardians at Fenway Park, was not of major significance.
Of greater note was the how — and what those trends may portend heading into the most important time of year: another ugly outing for reliever Erik Miller, and another night of minimal hitting for the lineup.
The Red Sox (84-73) have dropped three games in a row and eight of their past 12.
“We’ve still got five games to play, and you [have to] keep guys out there and engaged and ready to roll,” manager Chad Tracy said. “I told the guys before, we earned the right to be in position to be able to line things up. That being said, we still want to go out and win the games. We had a chance to tonight.”
Miller inherited a tied game in the ninth inning and struggled again, allowing a game-deciding run and throwing 22 pitches (10 strikes). He hit his first batter, Chase DeLauter, with a pitch. DeLauter eventually scored on Nathaniel Lowe’s sacrifice fly. Altogether, Miller yielded two hits and a walk.
In September, the Sox’ theoretical top lefthanded setup man has one clean inning in seven attempts, a 8.53 ERA, and a 2.37 WHIP.
Miller said his patience with himself — and a mechanical issue he is trying to fix — is “definitely running thin at this point.”
“I’d be lying if I say otherwise,” he said. “I would like to have been through this by now, be over it. But … there’s no way I can feel better and work through it without throwing [in] a game. So that’s just how it’s going to have to be: keep throwing, get through it.”
Tracy, noting that Miller will pitch in a couple more games before the regular season ends Sunday, added: “I thought today was even another step in the right direction.”
Offensively, the Red Sox had few highlights. Mickey Gasper launched a pinch-hit tying home run off setup man Hunter Gaddis to lead off the eighth, but the Sox totaled nine runners stranded on base and went 0 for 9 with men in scoring position.
In the positives column: Adley Rutschman finished 3 for 4, with two doubles (and a line out to deep center) coming against lefthanders.
Entering the game, Rutschman was 2 for 26 with no extra-base hits against lefties as a member of the Red Sox.
“Being a switch hitter has a lot that goes into it, and you go through phases where you’re hitting good [from] one side and not the other and it flip flops sometimes and then goes back,” Rutschman said. “I want to be in a good spot, especially with the playoffs coming up.”
In a matchup between perhaps the top two rookie pitchers this year, Payton Tolle (5⅔ innings, two runs) was almost equal to fellow lefthander Parker Messick (five innings, one run) of the Guardians.
Tolle slogged through a 22-pitch second frame, during which he allowed three hits and two walks but managed to hold the AL Central-leading Guardians (82-75) to the two runs.
When Tracy pulled him in the sixth, Tolle walked off the Fenway mound — for potentially the last time this year — to a standing ovation from the fans behind the home dugout. He waved back to them.
“I think he’s won them over pretty significantly,” Tracy said.
Tolle finished his rookie season with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148⅔ innings (26 starts).
Up next: a start in the AL Wild Card Series.
“It’s the postseason. This is what we play for,” Tolle said. “But it is what it is. We go on, and we have a job to do.”

BOSTON -- When Payton Tolle walked off the mound with two outs in the top of the sixth inning on Tuesday night, it was the perfect opportunity for the Fenway faithful to recognize the power lefty for an outstanding rookie season.
Next time Tolle pitches, the noise is likely to be even louder, and not nearly as favorable.
The Red Sox will have no hesitation sending out the confident, charismatic 23-year-old into enemy territory.
While this was far from the best (5 2/3 innings, 8 hits, 2 ER, 2 BBs, 5 K’s) of Tolle’s 26 regular-season starts, it was more than enough to keep the Red Sox in the game.
Assuming Tolle doesn’t pitch again in the regular season, his final stat line includes this: A 3.03 ERA, 171 strikeouts, 40 walks, 1.10 WHIP and a .222 opponents batting average.
Playing short-handed without Willson Contreras (bruised knuckle, right hand), Ceddanne Rafaela (right quadriceps strain, 10-day IL) and Trevor Story (rest), the Red Sox continued their recent trend of not scoring much.
There were two bright spots.
Mickey Gasper came up as a pinch-hitter and hammered a game-tying solo shot to right in the bottom of the eighth.
Adley Rutschman, who had been slumping of late, belted two doubles as part of a three-hit night.

item.content:encoded:
For all intents and purposes, none of these last games down the stretch mean anything to the Red Sox. They have already punched their ticket to the playoffs and nothing that happens from here on out will change that.
But while readying themselves for the games that matter, the Red Sox would still prefer to go into the postseason with some momentum, and Tuesday’s performance was at times pretty hard to watch.
Playing without three projected postseason starters, the Red Sox suffered a listless 3-2 loss in their series opener against the Cleveland Guardians. Despite a game-tying pinch hit home run by Mickey Gasper in the bottom of the eighth, the Red Sox gave the lead right back in the ninth, capping off a night riddled with poor decisions and uncharacteristic mistakes.
Reliever Erik Miller saw his struggles continue by allowing two hits, a walk, a hit batsman and the go-ahead sacrifice fly by Angel Martinez in the top of the ninth, and outside of Gasper and Adley Rutschman going 3 for 4 with two doubles and a run scored, there wasn’t much to write home about as the Red Sox suffered their third straight defeat.
Making his final start before the playoffs, Payton Tolle wasn’t as sharp as he would’ve hoped, but once again he gave the Red Sox a chance to win.
After posting a scoreless first, Tolle allowed two runs and five baserunners over the course of a challenging second inning. He started by giving up a leadoff double, had a soft grounder from David Fry deflect off his leg and into the outfield for an RBI single, and allowed another single and a walk to load the bases with nobody out.
Tolle was able to minimize the damage from there, allowing a second run to score on a double play ball by Brayan Rocchio before escaping the inning. He continued facing traffic for the rest of his outing but grinded his way into the sixth and departed to a standing ovation from the Fenway Park faithful.
Tolle finished with two runs allowed on eight hits, two walks and a hit batsman over 5 2/3 innings with five strikeouts. He fell one out short of recording another quality start, leaving him with 13 in 26 outings, and he ends his rookie year with a 3.03 ERA and 171 strikeouts in 148 2/3 innings.
The Red Sox got a run back in the bottom of the second after Adley Rutschman led off with a double and came around to score on an RBI groundout by Andruw Monasterio, but otherwise the bats struggled against Guardians rookie Parker Messick. The left-hander, who came into the game with a 2.57 ERA and projects as a possible AL Cy Young Award finalist, limited the Red Sox to one run on five hits over five innings.
One thing Boston was able to do was drive up the rookie’s pitch count, particularly in the fourth when Monasterio was able to work a 12-pitch walk. That helped force the lefty from the game after five, giving the Red Sox a chance to try their luck against Cleveland’s bullpen.
The Red Sox let a golden opportunity go to waste in the bottom of the sixth, leaving men at second and third, but Alec Gamboa kept it a one-run game in the top of the seventh despite the Guardians taking advantage of some sloppy baseball to get runners at second and third themselves with one out.
Cleveland’s Fry, who had already grounded into a fielder’s choice where the runner was thrown out at the plate earlier in the third inning, did so a second time for the second out of the seventh, and Gamboa struck out former No. 1 overall pick Travis Bazzana to end the inning.
Then, in the bottom of the eighth, Gasper struck for his 10th home run of the season, hitting the first pitch he saw from Guardians reliever Hunter Gaddis 390 feet to the right field stands.
The good vibes didn’t last long.
Miller, who had proven an impactful bullpen addition since his arrival at the trade deadline, saw his recent control issues continue with his latest ugly outing. The left-hander hit the first batter he faced, gave up the lead on a sacrifice fly by Martinez and eventually loaded the bases before getting a fly out to keep things from spiraling further.
Miller has now allowed six runs and six walks over his past 3 1/3 innings, a trend the Red Sox can’t afford to continue if he’s to remain a high-leverage option in the playoffs.

item.title: [bostonherald.com] How Red Sox reached ‘natural conclusion’ to keep Chad Tracy as manager
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Starr
item.description: There were no guarantees on the night of April 25, when Chad Tracy was abruptly pulled from what ultimately became his 499th and final win as Triple-A Worcester manager, and handed the keys to Boston’s big-league kingdom on an interim basis. Nor the next morning when Tracy, 41, walked into the Camden Yards visitors’ clubhouse in Baltimore to manage his first big-league game, to stunned and upset Red Sox players publicly questioning the future of the organization after the previous night’s firing
item.content:encoded:
There were no guarantees on the night of April 25, when Chad Tracy was abruptly pulled from what ultimately became his 499th and final win as Triple-A Worcester manager, and handed the keys to Boston’s big-league kingdom on an interim basis.
Nor the next morning when Tracy, 41, walked into the Camden Yards visitors’ clubhouse in Baltimore to manage his first big-league game, to stunned and upset Red Sox players publicly questioning the future of the organization after the previous night’s firing of longtime manager Alex Cora and six coaches.
The future became clearer on Tuesday morning. Hours before opening the final homestand of 2026, and fresh off clinching a playoff spot for the second consecutive year, the Red Sox officially announced Tracy’s new three-year contract to become their 49th manager, and the exercising of their 2029 and 2030 options on chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.
“When it became time to make the very difficult change in leadership with our major league team, there was kind of really only one name that was considered,” Breslow said as he, Tracy and team president and CEO Sam Kennedy sat in the Fenway Park interview room Tuesday afternoon to discuss the day’s news.
The Red Sox were 10-17, tied for the American League’s worst record, when Tracy arrived. And they got worse before they got better. They lost several stars to injuries in late April and early May, and fell to their worst home record to begin a season since 1932 in early June.
“I mean, it was abysmal,” Kennedy said. “April, May and June were brutal to live through.”
As the losses mounted, so did public perception of Tracy as a stalking horse, and Breslow as a man on borrowed time. But within the organization, Red Sox leadership and players felt a significant shift when Tracy took the reins.
“It became pretty clear early on that Chad was the right person at the right time to lead this group,” Breslow, 46, said. “(We) recognized that this was a fit we wanted to preserve. … I think there was probably some realization a few weeks ago, maybe even further, that there’s a natural conclusion here that we’re working toward.”
The question of Tracy’s future with the organization was present from the start, both internally and externally, but he remained unruffled.
“Yeah, I mean, it didn’t bother me much anyways,” Tracy said. “I worried about the players. I worried about getting us on track, helping get us on track. … That was what my focus was on, and I figured this stuff, if it goes well enough, it’ll come together on its own.”
Tracy took a similar approach to last offseason’s WooSox managerial contract negotiations. Many might try to make the leap to a major league coaching job after managing a Triple-A team to winning seasons in each of their four years at the helm, and spending over two decades playing and working in the minor leagues. But Tracy took the “Que Sera Sera” approach; whatever will be, will be.
“I think those opportunities happen on their own,” Tracy said. “You don’t operate in those jobs thinking about, how do I get to my next one? You just do your job. … I’m here to help people. I’m here to help the players. And if I do that properly, then whether it’s here or somewhere else, those things always take care of themselves.”
Tracy’s unbotheredness by limbo and chaos, and his ability to navigate turbulent waters and help his players do the same were key factors in the removal of the interim tag.
Asked what he learned about Tracy after moving him up to the majors, Breslow said, “The answer to that is maybe what makes Chad most remarkable, which is, he was exactly the same. He was exactly as he was as the manager in Worcester, he was exactly the same after a shutout win as he was a heart-wrenching defeat, and I think that stability, that consistency, is how our players have responded so well.
“So what I’ve learned is he is just an unbelievably intense but even-keeled leader, someone who builds sincere and authentic relationships with everyone that he interacts with and comes across, someone that I think can can be trusted to be honest and questioned when it’s appropriate to do so, and someone who is willing to always put the players in the organization first.”
Members of the Red Sox echoed Breslow’s sentiments.
“I’m happy for him, because he’s handled this amazingly,” veteran shortstop Trevor Story told the Herald. “Odds were kind of stacked against him, and kind of our team in general, too. So happy for him, and he deserves it. He stewarded the ship in an incredible way, so pumped for him that he can kick that interim tag and be here for a while.”
“He’s a real calming influence,” Story continued. “If you talk to him or get to know him at all, he’s very level-headed, really knowledgeable baseball guy, and just being around him is a good feeling. So that goes a long way, I think, to being a manager, and I think yeah, he’s shown that he can handle this whole situation of Boston and everything going on.”
“He’s done an incredible job, just bringing this clubhouse together, and just taking it one day at a time, and I am incredibly happy for him,” catcher and first baseman Mickey Gasper told the Herald. “There’s nobody that’s earned something more that I’ve been around in the game of baseball than Trace, getting this job. He’s done a tremendous job, and I couldn’t think of anybody else better for the role.”
“I’ve learned so much from him,” added Gasper, who played for Tracy on the ‘24 WooSox and split this season between Worcester and Boston. “How to be a baseball man around your teammates, how to bring a fresh slate every day to the ballpark.
“The wins and losses wear on you that day. Playing for Trace the last couple years, even in the minor leagues we’ve had some tough losses together, and he always comes back the next day. Today is a new day. This is the task at hand, and just being able to turn the page after tough spots, tough losses, just adversity in general. And I think just watching him go about his business that’s what I’ve learned the most. He leads by example.”
Those particular attributes also made Tracy an ideal partner for Breslow. The latter must make the difficult decisions, the former has proved adept at ensuring the ripple effects don’t become tsunamis. The Red Sox feel this pairing will provide the stability that has been in scarce supply over the last decade.
“It’s huge,” Kennedy said of locking in this tandem for the next three years. “It’s a sacred relationship, between the head of baseball operations and the manager. Being on the same page, having that trust, that confidence in each other (is) something that I’ve learned going back to my days at the New York Yankees and the San Diego Padres. And here, seeing successful versions of it, and seeing unsuccessful versions of it.
“Lord knows we’ve made mistakes in our time. And just ensuring that you have that relationship right is critical. So yeah, it’s great to have that stability now. And look, we haven’t achieved anything, we know that. But I think we’re set up for success going forward.”
Story was glad to say he felt differently than that morning in Baltimore, when he was one of several longtime Red Sox who wondered “what the true direction of the franchise is.”
“When AC and all the guys got let go, we didn’t know the direction,” Story said. “And now, I feel like we do.”

Sox slugger Mickey Gasper's motivation stems from his roots in Merrimack
Merrimack's Mickey Gasper has become a fan favorite at Fenway Park, with his baseball journey taking him from high school to the Nashua Silver Knights through the minor leagues and finally to the Boston Red Sox.
Gasper grew up in Merrimack, about an hour away from Fenway.
"For me, playing with a little chip on my shoulder helps me," he told News 9.
Gasper's story is familiar to Granite Staters now, but many still ask how he can go from playing T-ball to consistently hitting homers for the Red Sox.
"A lot of work," he said.
>> Download the free WMUR app to get updates on the go <<
That work ethic was taught by his parents, Livia and Mick, who moved from New Jersey to Merrimack in 2001 when Mickey was about 5 years old.
"He is tenacious, and the resilience started growing at a young age," Livia Gasper said.
"He was competitive in T-ball," his father said. "One day, he made a great play. The coach of the other team said, 'We don't play outs.' And Mickey is like (making an appalled expression)."
"If there's anything that somebody from the Northeast does, it's that you do play with a chip on your shoulder," Mickey Gasper said. "A lot of people have doubted my process just in the last two years."
"He had bunk beds in his room, and I found it taped up on the flat, and it says, 'I'm not good enough,'" his father said.
Mickey Gasper worked to become good enough to play for the Merrimack High School Tomahawks.
"A lot of elite high school players rely on talent. He never did," said Nick Jaskolka, his high school coach. "That's a rare makeup for a high-end player."
That makeup has been put to the test. Mickey Gasper is currently having a breakout season at 30 years old in his second stint with the Red Sox.
Two years ago, he made his major league debut with Boston after more than five years in the minors. His family was in the stands for the first few games, making the trip from New Jersey, where they moved from New Hampshire in 2019.
But Gasper went 0-for-18 and was sent back down to the minors.
"We actually have not been back to Boston," his mother said.
"I'm staying away from Boston," his father said. "I feel like I was the kiss of death."
What has happened in Boston this summer is nothing short of remarkable. Recalled from AAA on Aug. 17, Mickey Gasper hit his first home run in a Red Sox uniform two years after his debut.
It was the first of three straight games with a homer -- six in 12 games -- for one of the best months in the history of baseball. His stats were up there with the likes of Ted Williams and Barry Bonds.
"It's cool," Mickey Gasper said. "It's something you can't live on. It's a month's stretch."
On the bottom of the bat he used to get all those hits is a picture of him and his father.
"It's very humbling," his father said. "It's been a lifelong love for baseball."
Despite that amazing run, he was sent back down on Saturday, Aug. 29. He didn't have to report to Worcester until the following Tuesday, so he visited his parents.
"First thing I said was, I'm going to go back to Freehold for the day just to be able to spend time with them," he said.
"We definitely felt the heaviness," his mother said. "We were actually supposed to go to the game on Sunday. I made a big old vat of sauce and meatballs."
"Short pasta. Against my request," Mickey Gasper said. "I like spaghetti. I'm a spaghetti guy."
This AAA stint was shorter than the pasta his mom made. During that dinner, Mickey Gasper's phone was ringing. It was the Red Sox on the other end, saying he was going back up. In his first at-bat, he hit another home run.
"He makes good meatballs," his father said.
"We go together from what feels like the lowest of lows to the highest of highs, and on that day, it was in a span of 12 hours," his mother said. "We were in tears."
"I thank my family for everything. Just being around them is…," Mickey Gasper said before trailing off.
Mickey Gasper's efforts helped the Red Sox clinch a playoff spot. Like him, the team turned things around this year. The Sox were 14 games below .500 in late June, and if the season ended today, they would play a best-of-three Wild Card series at Yankee Stadium, where his parents have been this year.
Mick and Livia Gasper could bring the pasta and meatballs to him next time.
